speechtext:
Order. I have a short statement dealing with a question of procedure which I think it would be in order to make at this time. As appears in Votes and Proceedings of yesterday the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) presented the fourth report of the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills which read as follows:
Your committee has considered Bill S-15, an act to incorporate The Good News Broadcasting Association of Canada, and has agreed to report the preamble thereof not proven on the grounds that the committee feels that it would not be appropriate in the circumstances outlined to the committee to issue a federal charter.
Thereafter, as reported in yesterday's Hansard at pages 2292 and 2293, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) proposed the following motion:
That Bill No. S-15 as reported be referred back to the committee on miscellaneous private bills for reconsideration.
At that point Mr. Speaker intervened to suggest to the hon. member that the proper time to move such a motion would be during the private bills period if the bill was then before the house. Later on the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka stated that under the rules, especially standing order 110, this bill would not be placed on the order paper, and this would prohibit the bill in question being placed upon the orders of the day during the private members' hour. At this juncture Mr. Speaker suggested that the matter be postponed until today to give him the opportunity of going into the matter.
May I be permitted to say that I have considered the matter and to reiterate that it was not the proper time for the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka to propose his motion to refer back the bill under routine proceedings, as he did yesterday, since the bill had first to be placed upon the orders of the day by special order of the house. In this connection standing order 110 applies.
In looking at two precedents relating to similar instances-the first in 1931, at page 552 of the Journals and page 3824 of Hansard;
the second in 1958, at page 401 of the Journals and page 3329 of Hansard-it will be seen that a motion should be moved and adopted under routine proceedings in order to place such a bill upon the orders of the day for consideration, and the motion to refer the bill back to the committee is dealt with at its proper place when private bills are taken up during the hour for private members' business.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that pursuant to the recommendations of the Norris report regarding possible prosecutions, special counsel will be appointed immediately to review all the facts and advise whether charges should be laid against any persons for conspiracy to prevent, by unlawful means, persons from working in the business of shipping; or for conspiracy to commit indictable offences, particularly offences involving violence; or for offences under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
At the appropriate stage I would envisage that there would be consultation with the appropriate provincial authorities in regard to any Criminal Code infractions indicated by the advice of such counsel.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED STATES TAX ON INTERNATIONAL CAPITAL TRANSACTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the message which the President of the United States delivered to congress at noon today is directed towards the improvement of the international balance of payments of the United States. One of the measures to which the President referred was action yesterday by the international monetary fund to facilitate continued investment by the fund in United States dollars. The arrangement is quite a technical one and I shall not try to describe it at this time. The effect is simply to allow the fund's holdings of U.S. dollars to continue to increase as they have done in the last two or three years.
Another measure announced by the President involves a system of taxes on certain international capital transactions. Certain types of capital movements have been causing weakness in the U.S. balance of payments and the new tax system is apparently designed to meet this problem. The tax applies to U.S. nationals who purchase securities, both bonds and stocks, of the following countries: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Federal Republic of Germany, Hong Kong, Italy, Japan, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Monaco, The Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Republic of South Africa, San Marino, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom.
The tax rate proposed ranges from per cent of the value of securities with a maturity of three to three and a half years and rises to 15 per cent in the cases of securities with a maturity of 28J years or more. The same 15 per cent applies to purchases of shares. Perhaps I might just read into the record the three paragraphs relating to this particular tax:
The interest equalization tax would be a special temporary excise tax, to remain in effect through 1965, imposed on the acquisition of stock, securities or other obligations of foreign issuers or depository receipts or other evidence of interest in, or rights to acquire, such interests. The tax would be payable by all United States citizens, residents and corporations, including organizations exempt from federal income taxes. The tax would apply to portfolio purchases of stock or debt securities issued by foreign corporations, governments, or other persons, whether such securities represented new or already outstanding issues and whether the acquisition was effected in the United States or abroad. It would not apply, however, to purchases of interest presently held by Americans.
18, 1963
U.S. Tax on International Capital
The tax would not be applicable to direct investments by United States persons in overseas subsidiaries or affiliates, nor would it apply to acquisition of any indebtedness payable upon demand or maturing in less than three years. Moreover, loans made by commercial banks in the ordinary course of their banking business would be exempted. The tax would not be applied to purchases of securities issued by international organizations of which the United States is a member, governments of countries considered to be less developed, and corporations whose principal activities are centred in less developed countries. An underwriter or dealer would be exempted from the tax on acquisitions of stock or obligations resold to foreigners as part of the underwriting of a new issue.
The tax would be applied to acquisitions occurring after the date of the President's message. It would not apply to purchase commitments made on the open market on or before that date or to other purchases which the buyer on that date was unconditionally obligated to make. Exemption from the tax would also be provided for purchases made within 60 days after the date of the President's message if the security purchased were covered by a registration statement filed with the securities and exchange commission within 90 days prior to the date of the President's message.
Now, Mr. Speaker, quite clearly the measures proposed by the President of the United States will have wide repercussions in each of the 22 countries I have mentioned. These repercussions, if the President's proposals are approved by congress, may well have an important effect upon Canada's balance of payments and upon the Canadian economy as a whole. It would be unwise for me to say more than this, however, until there has been time to give careful study and consideration to all the implications of the President's proposals.

I think this proposition made by President Kennedy is close to another proposition which was made in this house about a month ago when the Minister of Finance presented his budget. At that time he imposed a tax of 30 per cent on the sale of Canadian stocks or shares to foreign purchasers. (Translation):
At that time, Mr. Speaker, we had in Canada a Mr. Kierans who went to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to ask him to withdraw the tax on the sale of Canadian securities to non-residents. Today we hope that the same Mr. Kierans will go and see President Kennedy to ask him to withdraw that tax too.
Mr. Speaker, I notice however that even if the tax applies exactly on the same grounds as the one the Minister of Finance had introduced on June 13 last only to withdraw it a few days later, this time, instead of the Canadian government getting the profit, it will be the American government which will collect this tax on the sale of securities, and, once again, Canadians will be victimized.
I am sure that when the Minister of Finance spoke to us about administrative difficulties, there were none; but the American government intended to impose that tax today. The under-secretary of state exerted some pressure on the Minister of Finance for the withdrawal of the tax, so that the American government might impose it now on exactly the same items.
At that time the Minister of Finance spoke of technicalities and of technical difficulties. Today, he again mentions technicalities. There are no such technicalities. It is the Canadian government which, once again, complies with demands of American finance.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance said, and rightly so, that this might affect the balance of payments, but I think that, as we Canadians will certainly benefit less from the influx of American capital in this country, and shall have less American investments here, I think this would be the time

for the Minister of Finance to find some sources of capital, to create capital in our own country, so that investments do not decrease and that we continue to develop this country with our own capital, because we shall no longer be able to count on American capital investments.
The Minister of Finance should see things more clearly now that he has been taken in by the American government, and he should learn from that lesson that he cannot count on foreign countries helping Canada-on the contrary we are their victim-and he should see to it that we, in Canada, use our own capital resources to develop this country.
Americans also have their own sources of capital, and they use them, not only for the expansion of their country, but for developing other parts of the world. Canada should do the same thing. This country should get from the Bank of Canada the capital it needs for its development, and then it will have no more cause to complain about decisions made by foreign countries.

Mr. Speaker, as the spokesman for the Conservative party has said, this is a most serious statement that the Minister of Finance has had to make to us. However, I think it would be extremely naive to imagine that Mr. Kennedy has taken this action because of the actions of the Canadian government. I think that is perhaps exaggerating our importance in the world.
It is, however, a situation that the government should have been able to foresee in the light of the continuing stream of reports for many weeks past of the grave concern of the United States authorities over the continuing drain on their gold reserves and the appeals that were made by President Kennedy to United States investors to withhold further transfers of capital to Europe in particular to West Germany, for one.
I foresee that the government is going to face some very serious problems with regard to our exchange rate. If they attempt in the face of this move on the part of the United States authorities to maintain the fixed exchange rate and to pursue the minister's professed goal of a balanced budget, we are going to find that the Canadian people will have to pay a very bitter price for it.
I suggest that the government should now reconsider its whole attitude toward an expansionist policy in this country at this time. It may very well be that the crisis that has

been precipitated by the United States administration will cause the industrialized countries in the world to take seriously the proposals that have been made for the developing of a much greater measure of international liquidity than at present obtains. If so, then there will be some gain made from this situation.

SUGGESTED DISCREPANCY IN ANSWERS GIVEN
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Defence Production to a discrepancy which is revealed in yesterday's Hansard. On page 2298 we find an answer given by the hon. gentleman to a question asked on the subject of exercise Tocsin B. The question was:
Was exercise Tocsin B carried out in the fall of 1981? If so, how many Soviet bombers were assumed to have taken part in this simulated attack?
The answer given was:
As the exercise did not involve interceptor forces it was not necessary to assume any specific number of enemy bombers.
I should like to point out that in a return to an order of the house brought down on February 12, 1962, on a motion of Mr. Pit-


man there was a reply to a question asking "What was the extent of the simulated attack in terms of (e) bombers attacking?" The reply states, among other things:
For exercise purposes it was assumed that 300 to 350 individual aircraft tracks were detected in the attack on North America.
Those two answers are certainly at variance. While I think it is serious enough to withhold information, I think it is even more serious when we are given information which contradicts information previously given in the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Defence Production):
subtopic: SUGGESTED DISCREPANCY IN ANSWERS GIVEN
speechtext:
I think the difference is more
apparent than real. The question asked was how many bombers? The answer given to Mr. Pitman was, none; not a given number of bombers, but individual aircraft tracks. This means tracks on radar screens, and one bomber passing over a series of radar observation points might produce as many as 20 or 30 tracks. So the number of bombers and the number of tracks are not necessarily the same. I think the information given to the hon. member was correct. No specific number of bombers either had to be assumed or was assumed.

subtopic: SUGGESTED DISCREPANCY IN ANSWERS GIVEN
speechtext: On the question of privilege, if the hon. gentleman is correct the first answer was wrong, because the return to the order dated February 9, 1962 was specific. Question 5 asked: "What was the extent of the simulated attacks in terms of (e) bombers attacking?" The question did not have to do with tracks at all, and the answer was in reference to bombers attacking.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a comprehensive pension program to be known as the Canada pension plan and to provide among other things for the payment of pensions on an adjusted scale commencing at the option of the pensioner, at any age between 65 and 70 years; for the payment of pensions to surviving spouses commencing at any age after 65 years; for the progressive establishment of such pensions over an initial period averaging ten years in order to facilitate the adjustment of existing pension schemes to the new plan; for the payment of an additional pension of ten dollars a month to all persons to whom a pension may be paid under the Old Age Security Act; for the adjustment of pensions payable under the Old Age Security Act to co-ordinate such pensions with the new plan; and for the appointment and remuneration of such officers, clerks and employees as may be required for the due carrying out of the new plan; and to provide further that all expenditures under the new plan, additional to those required under the Old Age Security Act, shall be paid out of or reimbursed from contributions by employees, employers and self-employed persons.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CANADA PENSION PLAN, INCREASED OLD AGE SECURITY PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
In rising today to introduce this resolution dealing with the Canada pension plan I have the honour to speak to the implementation of one of the most important

and far reaching plans of action put forward by this or any other government. It is the natural next step in providing rounded welfare legislation for Canada. The whole record of the Liberal party in office has always been the introduction of legislation designed for the welfare of Canadians. Every major social advance made by parliament in this century has been made under a Liberal government. The legislation now before us, I am proud to say, will continue this tradition.
I should like briefly to express my personal gratitude to members of the public service for their devotion to duty and the long hours they have given to the development of this plan. Nor should I forget to say a word about the contribution of many of Canada's pension experts who, from the depths of the years of their experience, have offered advice and admonition to me, to my officials and to many members of the house who have been kind enough to bring their submissions to me.
The purpose of the Canada pension plan is to ensure, as was said in the speech from the throne, that all Canadians will have an opportunity to retire in security and with dignity. The legislation based upon this resolution is complex. Legislation as far reaching as this, as much a departure from the past as this is, must be drawn to produce its benefits as early as possible to achieve its goals without interfering with the body politic. Further, the parliamentary process, which was designed as a way in which all the people's representatives might take their part in such decisions, must be used in this case to full advantage.
In my view, Mr. Chairman, it is the government's responsibility to propose a scheme. It is then the responsibility of all members of parliament as the people's representatives to address themselves, without thought of partisan advantage-

You have already been
partisan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CANADA PENSION PLAN, INCREASED OLD AGE SECURITY PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
-to the proposal; to modify, to amplify or to change, but always to act with the intent to cause improvement in the legislation. Each of us here has a responsibility to produce the best piece of legislation possible in every field. This is especially so when the legislation is such as that to which this resolution refers, legislation which will for the future affect almost every Canadian. For that reason I make no apology for saying that the contributory pension plan to which this government has bound itself is inflexible only in its main purpose. The government will therefore welcome from any member any contribution or suggestion genuinely designed to improve the legislation, particularly

as all other parties have already committed themselves to the principle and idea of contributory pensions.
I recall that in my early months in the house the then minister of justice, Mr. Fulton, took such an attitude and saw fit to adopt a couple of suggestions of mine which were then incorporated in legislation respecting capital and non-capital murder. Indeed, this co-operative attitude has been shown already in the government's approval in principle of several private members' bills which have been referred for study to committee.
I think it is fair to say to all hon. members that the government's pension scheme, introduced now so quickly after the opening of this session of parliament, has excited throughout the body politic a great deal of interest. The fact that the plan is intended in its application to cover the widest possible range of citizens is itself sufficient cause for this interest. Most economically advanced countries of the world have been moving toward this type of contributory wage related pension scheme for some time. The introduction in 1951 by the Liberal government of the day of the old age security program brought into effect in Canada, as all hon. members know, a flat rate scheme available to all at the age of 70 without a means test.
The present premier of Quebec had a lot to do with that plan. The present Secretary of State for External Affairs had a lot more to do with it. It was a logical and particularly apt step for pensions in Canada at that time. Unfortunately, however, in recent years some of the increases in payments made under this legislation have been based not upon increase in productivity, not upon progress of the economy, but only upon pure political expediency. This can no longer be countenanced.

speechtext:
Those who cry courtesy might have the courtesy to wait until I have concluded to ask their questions. As I say, it is degrading to those who are recipients of old age security to find themselves used as political footballs, and it is arrant fiscal irresponsibility if such payments are not keyed to the progress of the economy. The country simply cannot continue to afford to pay attractive sums which have no reason for being except for their political sex appeal. Present old age security payments yield at best little more than subsistence levels. Our country has always recognized, through adopting the old age security legislation, the validity of that oldest of social responsibilities, that we support the aged of our community.
In a modern industrial society it is increasingly impossible for a family to care for its own aged. Of course, it is rejected by all Canadians that those who cannot be cared for by their immediate families should be shunted aside to fall upon public assistance, or worse, to be abandoned. Some may criticize the type of plan which we propose under this resolution because it is one where the contributor, while active in the working population, pays to the government to create a debt from the state to him for his own retirement years. In effect, under this plan each generation will provide for the one which has preceded it in building Canada. No matter in what way pensions are provided, this is in fact their economic and social significance.
As I mentioned earlier, all the major parties have already committed themselves in principle to a wage related contributory pension scheme. What then, one may ask, are the alternatives in designing such a scheme? Each party has gone on record, reflecting the generally held feeling in this country, that such a scheme must be comprehensive so that it applies to the widest possible group of Canadians, and it must be as inexpensive as possible while returning an adequate pension to the individual. It must be truly portable or transferable so that an individual Canadian may carry his benefits with him anywhere he may choose to live and work.
It is possible, Mr. Chairman, to construct a scheme which, in common with many of those offered by private pension companies, is completely funded; but this would put in the hands of the state tremendous sums of money which would be withdrawn or

Canada Pension Plan
used lor other purposes. No government plans are completely funded. In a public plan the contributor may rely upon the fact that so long as his country exists the continuous inflow of contributions under such a plan will assure him of his benefit rights on his retirement. These were the arguments balanced by the government in coming to its conclusion that this plan should not be funded; thus the plan is framed on a pay as you go basis. The plan, including the costs of administration, will be no charge at all upon the general revenue.
The Canada pension plan has important features which are new to this country. We cannot tell at this stage exactly how people will decide to use them. For example, we do not know how soon and in what numbers people will take advantage of the opportunity to start pensions before the age of 70. Nor do we know how many voluntary contributors will decide to take part in the plan. Neither of these factors affects the finances of the scheme in the long run. Whatever the decisions, the relation of benefits to earnings will settle out in a way that makes it safe to estimate that for the first 10 years the contribution rate will not need to be more than 2 per cent of earnings.
However, the calculations for the next few years are more uncertain. The ages people choose to begin pensions, and the number of volunteers who join, will have a relatively big effect on the short run finances of the scheme. Also, of course, the amount of time which parliament decides to take in discussing the legislation will influence the date at which collection of contributions starts, and therefore the contribution rate needed to finance the increase to $75 in the flat rate pension. Until there has been some preliminary discussion of this, Mr. Chairman, it is not proposed to set the exact date for starting the $10 increase to $75.

May I say that I hope, sir, it will be early in 1964, to the disappointment of the hon. member for Brome-Missis-quoi. Because of the uncertainty as to the length of time the house may take in dealing with the matter, the government cannot yet fix the initial contribution rate more precisely than to say it will not be more than 2 per cent of earnings. Here I refer again to the total rate which will be divided between employers and employees. The rate for the employee alone will be not more than 1 per

cent, that is to say, a man whose annual earnings are $3,000 will pay up to $2.50 per month. The maximum contribution for anyone earning $4,000 a year or more will be not more than $3.33 per month.
It was decided at an early stage of the pension plan that a combination of compulsory and voluntary coverage would be the most acceptable and most workable method of achieving comprehensive coverage. How, then, to operate the comprehensive plan? Fortunately, Mr. Chairman, machinery already exists. As all hon. members are aware there is this machinery in the combined resources of the Department of National Revenue, my department and the unemployment insurance commission. It was decided, therefore, that this same machinery should, for simplicity, efficiency and cheapness, be utilized for registration at the time of the regular reissuing of unemployment insurance books and numbers by the unemployment insurance commission. This will also have the advantage that this same numbering system may be used.
Accordingly, since the next time for renumbering and reissuing the books has been scheduled for May 1964, it was concluded that the registration for contributors should be carried out at that time. This, Mr. Chairman, is the earliest practicable time, bearing in mind the tremendous administrative complexities of registering what is expected to be more than seven million contributors.
Then the coverage of this scheme, the Canada pension plan, is of every Canadian who can be included, bearing in mind some administrative problems. Broadly speaking, the only classes definitely excluded from coverage are those whose earnings are paid to them by their own spouses, for obvious reasons, members of the armed forces and casual employees. Employees of provincial governments may be included if the province so wishes, as may employees of foreign governments and international agencies.
The Canada pension plan is designed to pay benefits related to earnings. As all hon. members know, wages are not uniform across the length and breadth of our country. What is less than sufficient for subsistence in one part of the country may provide a much greater degree of comfort for the recipient in another part of the country. For that reason we should have no difficulty in agreeing here in committee that the pension plan should be one which upon retirement provides an income, bearing in mind the reduced costs of living on retirement, related to that enjoyed throughout an individual's productive life. This scheme is designed to do just that.
We already have in this country a flat rate scheme. The new wage related scheme is added

to it, and payments will be made in one lump sum of the two portions of pension, flat rate and wage related. This will mean that our retired, rather than as now supplementing the flat rate payment of $65 per month with their savings, if any, or public assistance, will have in the future an appreciably more generous income related to their earnings, up to an average level. It is, unhappily, not possible to apply this retroactively to all those who have taken or who are about to take their retirement. For this reason, and in order to provide a little more in the way of security for those who have now retired or will shortly be retiring, this government has pledged itself to the payment, from the contributions to this plan, of an additional $10 per month to each recipient of old age security.

speechtext:
In proceeding to tell the truth about this plan, as about all other things, it must be readily apparent, even to those such as the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) who obviously from his remarks knows so little about the field, that if payment of contributions were started immediately it would not be possible tomorrow to pay out, to anyone reaching retirement age, the full benefits of such a plan which has the aim of providing sufficient sums to enable people to retire in security and dignity. There has to be a period of earnings before benefits can be related to

Canada Pension Plan
earnings. There will be, as we have said throughout in our plans, ten years from its inception to the payment of full benefits, and this will permit the adjustment of pension plans already in existence. In the interim each person retiring will be paid a graduated sum, based upon the length and the amount of his or her contributions, plus the flat rate of $75 benefit.
It is increasingly common that those who are employed by others cease their employment and take their retirement at an age earlier than 70. For this reason, and in order to bridge the gap between earning and retirement years, the government has designed the plan to provide an option to each pensioner to draw his or her pension on a reduced rate from the age of 65 onward. It is anticipated that such options will begin at the earliest possible date, in January 1966.
There are those who will ask, why not start the contributions now? This would, of course, permit for earlier payments to all, but I suppose it need not be pointed out to hon. members of experience that the parliamentary system itself takes time for the preparation, discussion and passage of such legislation. It should be borne in mind that this is a highly complex scheme and requires a great deal of unseen administrative work, all very time consuming, and none of which may be commenced until parliament has given approval to the full legislative scheme. Forms and literature must be designed, tenders called and material produced. Forms must be prepared by punching for mass registration and setting up of pension records. Then these will have to be distributed to the U.I.C. offices. Forms will have to be distributed to an estimated 350,000 employers. Temporary field staffs have to be recruited and trained to complete this phase. A master key punching of about 7 million account records has to be completed, and after that the numbers and forms must be distributed to employers, some of whom will have to redesign their payroll records before they start paying the contributions.
The machinery of government, which I have already mentioned and which is already in being, has to be used because of the otherwise tremendous outlay and delay, and we have to use it without interfering with the regular responsibilities of the U.I.C. offices in looking after the unemployed and paying unemployment claims, together with the regular responsibilities of national revenue in the income tax field.
All these considerations place the earliest date for the commencement of payment of contributions at October, 1964, and this only if this legislation is treated with dispatch by this house. Normally one would only anticipate payment of the increased old age pensions to
IMiss LaMarsh.]
be made after these contributions have begun to flow in, after October, 1964. However it is contemplated that the contributions, once started, will produce enough revenue within a fiscal period to enable payments to start very early in 1964.
I can see a question in some hon. members' eyes; just how much will the pension benefits be? Average earnings in the country are approximately $4,000 per year, and for this reason this figure has been chosen as the starting level. All earnings up to this level will be used in computing contributions. The plan is designed, when the transition period of 10 years is over, to pay a pension of 30 per cent of the earnings upon which contributions have been made, if taken at the age of 70, and upon a reduced basis if taken at any time from 65 to 69.
This basis has been so designed that the average person will receive the same total payment from the age he starts his pension until his death, whichever starting age he chooses. His lifetime earnings will be the basis for the scale of the payments, and here is a most important feature. The average of these earnings will be adjusted by an index representing the general level of salaries and wages, so that he will be receiving benefits on the basis of the equivalent receipt of earnings in the year of his retirement. The effect will be that the Canada pension plan will permanently provide a satisfactory standard of pension for those with earnings up to the average level. This $4,000 level will be adjusted with changes in the general level of wages and salaries, and will do away with the incentive to barter for the favour of the old people of this country just before an election.
When the plan has passed its transition stage a man whose wage has been $4,000 or more will receive a monthly income related pension at age 70 of $100 plus the flat rate portion, totalling $175 per month. If his wife is also a contributor she will receive up to the same amount. If a man and his wife, both contributors, choose instead to retire at age 65, each will receive up to $118 per month in pension.
What of the widow and widower? There is here, some hon. members will be pleased to know, complete equality, and each spouse receives the same treatment regardless of sex. Either survivor of a marriage may be sure of receiving somewhat more than half the retirement income of man and wife together. This, of course, applies to survivors of 65 years or over.
It might be of some interest to hon. members to compare the relative benefits of the United States social security plan with those of the

Canada pension plan. In each case, at present levels, this proposed Canadian plan is more generous than the United States plan. It should be borne in mind that the figures which I will be using are of retirement at the age of 65. Our benefits are greater at the age of 70 years, as I previously explained-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CANADA PENSION PLAN, INCREASED OLD AGE SECURITY PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
May I thank hon. members for their courtesy in allowing me to complete my remarks, Mr. Chairman. The table to which I made reference indicates that for average monthly earnings of $100-and this, of course, is at the end of the transition period, when the plan is in full operation- in Canada benefits at age 65 will be $71; at age 70, $105, as compared with the United States benefits at the same income level of $59. At $200 monthly the Canadian benefit at age 65 will be $91; at age 70, $135, as compared with the United States benefit of $84. At $300 monthly the Canadian benefit at age 65 will be $111; at age 70, $165, as compared with the United States benefit of $105. Three hundred and thirty three dollars is the maximum level for monthly earnings. At that level Canadians will be able to obtain $175 a month if they are 70; $118 a month if they are 65. The upper limit of the United States pension plan at an income level of $333 per month is $112.
It will be seen from this scheme, Mr. Chairman, that this government has no intent to pre-empt the field of private planning for one's own retirement. There are many who will still wish to provide additional benefits over and above those to be provided under this plan. Indeed, the whole field above $4,000 in annual income is left open to private endeavour. It is obvious that in so far as these plans are concerned-that is, private pension plans, many of which are already in existence in Canada-employers and employees will have options either to keep them in existence, over and above the Canada pension plan, or to adjust them. What course will be followed in each instance is for the individual employer and his employees to decide, probably by negotiation. Since many such labour-management negotiations are for a period of one year or longer, it will be of advantage for us to provide specific information at the earliest possible date by the passage of this legislation.
Canada Pension Plan
Unfortunately this plan cannot provide for the wanted portability of private plans. In order to do this, at least upon a provincial basis, the province of Ontario has already enacted regulatory legislation and has expressed itself to be in accord with the goal of full portability of pension plans. Other provinces have been looking at this development with interest; they have expressed interest in this approach, so much so that some are now considering the adoption of similar plans. It is hoped that some uniformity might be obtained in order to make such private plans portable on a Canada-wide basis, just as will be this Canada pension plan by its very nature. However, the Ontario type of legislation, if enacted by each province of Canada, could not produce comprehensive coverage, nor could it provide quickly fair sized pensions for people of up to average earnings who retire in the next decade or two. Speaking from memory, Mr. Chairman, I believe it is some 40 years before the full benefit of the Ontario type regulatory plan could be obtained by an employee in that province.
The fact that this type of plan cannot provide benefits for those who retire in the near future appears to have been recognized in both Ontario and Quebec. On June 10 last the premier of Quebec expressed himself in his legislative assembly, when he was discussing pension schemes in answer to a question from the leader of the opposition there, as follows:
There are needs and attitudes which finally impose themselves in spite of what is said in constitutions. For instance, one cannot indefinitely deprive the population of a province of services from which it could constitutionally benefit from a central government if nothing equivalent is even offered to it.
Then on March 26 this year Mr. Cecile, the Ontario minister of welfare-my opposite number in that province-expressed his government's view in the legislative assembly in this way:
I have advocated for many years the inauguration of a compulsory social security maintenance scheme designed largely along the lines of the United States plan. I am pleased, indeed, to learn that the three major political parties in Canada are all agreed that not only is such a plan practical, but necessary. I hope the time is not too far distant when a social insurance scheme becomes effective in this country so that every working individual may obtain all the advantages that might be made available to a restricted group of employees under the more limited approach of a portable pension plan.
It seems to me that we in this house should take some cheer from this fact. I am sure this presages Ontario's full co-operation at the meeting of provincial premiers next week in bringing the benefits of the Canada pension plan to the people of Canada; if not from this government, perhaps from another.

Canada Pension Plan
In a country such as Canada, where there are concurrent areas of responsibility in the welfare field as in others, the closest cooperation between the federal government and the governments of the provinces is necessary for the social welfare of the Canadian people. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, it is known to all hon. members that there are other welfare programs in which the provinces and the federal government co-operate to provide joint action. For some time it has been apparent that these programs, the cost of which is in the main shared on a 50-50 basis, should be restudied with a view to fitting them to current conditions. In addition many provinces have their own independent welfare programs in which this government does not share in any way.
Of course this realm of action lies outside the scope of the Canada pension plan, but it cannot be ignored in a rounded welfare program for Canada. This is one of the important fields for discussion at the conference with the provinces which is to be held next week, and is a field referred to by the Prime Minister in his letter to the premiers of June 20 last. It is appreciated by the government that it is only fair to the provinces to consider the effect upon them of our moving ahead with this legislation. In particular, the increase in old age security payments to $75 will create a demand for parallel increases in shared programs which we have with the provinces. This will be one of the things we will wish to discuss. I hope, in another realm, that the provinces will look with favour on what I consider an area of need, and that is to provide an extension of assistance programs to single women and widows at age 60.

Mr. Chairman, a federal-provincial conference is especially necessary because there is another field where the close co-operation of the provinces and this government is most desirable. As a part of this Canada pension plan, ideally there would be provision in it for benefits to be paid at least to three classes of persons not now covered. There would be widows with dependant children; those contributors who, because they become disabled before reaching the age of 65 and no longer have regular earnings are now covered only by assistance programs, and orphans of contributors. It is now generally agreed that these are areas of need. Most provinces have indicated in the past a readiness to discuss plans for those in such circumstances. There is opinion that such programs, since they do not apply to "old age pensions"-that is the wording of the British North America Act-are not within the domain of the federal government,

and that legislation to deal with these cases on a Canada-wide basis would require amending our constitution upon the assent of the provinces. If agreement can be reached with the provinces-on these three types of classes, it is to be hoped that such provisions may soon be written into the Canada pension plan. This is an urgent matter for consultation with the provinces in the pension field.
In the time at my disposal today, Mr. Chairman, it has not been possible to deal fully with such a complex proposal as the Canada pension plan. Nor, I think we would all agree, is it fair to expect hon. members opposite to have a considered opinion on the basis of the resolution and these few remarks. Therefore, for the benefit of all hon. members and for the benefit of interested people in the country and the provincial governments, I have had prepared a supplementary outline of the nature and scope of the Canada pension plan. With the leave of the committee, Mr. Chairman, I would request that this outline be permitted to be printed as an appendix to Hansard. I am also prepared to send now to the leaders of each party a copy of this outline. I have as well a supply which might be tabled, printed in English and in French, which are available for any interested member. If leave of the committee is given, Mr. Chairman, then I should like at this time to have these documents distributed to interested members and I will table them accordingly.

I am not going to have any of these interruptions. I sat quietly while the hon. lady spoke and I am asking for the same consideration.
A moment ago, the hon. lady said something should be done for women-something should be done for unmarried women and widows. How far removed is this plan from the promise made in these words, to be found on page 11:
There is a serious gap in provisions for old age-one which particularly affects women workers. Many companies retire their women workers when they reach the age of 60 and the men at 65, but old age assistance is not available to anyone under the age of 65. For unmarried women and widows we would make it available at 60.
That was the promise. And that promise is being implemented today by undertakings to see whether the provinces will do what was promised in this policy summary to which I have referred.
I was interested in another aspect. One would almost think that creation began with the Liberal party-that nothing had ever been done in the field of social security except by the Liberal party. I do not intend to go into that today, except to say-

Oh, no, I am familiar with that old mythology, those myths which members opposite repeat over and over again until finally they begin to believe them themselves. No party has a monopoly of social justice. A short review of history from the days of Macdonald shows that throughout the years each political party has made its contribution in this regard. When I look back to the days of Macdonald I find that the Liberal party of that day opposed trade unions. They were entirely opposed to such a system being built up on behalf of labour. Does this mean that the Liberal party carries that stigma forever? As far as social security legislation is concerned, workmen's compensation provisions and the like, it was first introduced into the country by a Conservative government in the province of Ontario. After all, one would

think there was in the hearts of those so-called Liberals something different from what is possessed by other human beings.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CANADA PENSION PLAN, INCREASED OLD AGE SECURITY PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
One has only to state that proposition to understand how ridiculous it actually is. I repeat: This announcement today will prove a disappointment to the old people across this nation who were callously deceived by promises made during the election campaign by those who sit opposite.
I was tremendously interested in the homily on political honesty to which we were treated.
I felt the hon. lady did protest too much when she said that increases were based on other than political considerations. All I know is this: All through the election campaign the older people of this nation felt they had a true commitment from the Liberal party in this regard. They believed they had a commitment not only in general terms but in actuality. The hon. lady spoke of increases in the old age pension and social security payments as something which should be entirely based on economic considerations. What about 1957? You may remember, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. gentleman who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs took a strong stand at that time in this regard. The Prime Minister followed suit, because he was a member of that government. They were boasting of their surpluses; boasting of an expanding economy. The cost of living had been going up seriously and dangerously for five or six years. But they said at that time that $6 was enough for the old people of this nation. The economy at that time, so they said, was expanding. Yet at that very time they refused any further increase. All kinds of explanations were given. One of them was supplied by the Hon. Walter Harris, who was minister of finance. He said: If we give them more than $6 there will be a dangerous trend toward inflation. That was the excuse. They thought they could get away with it.
During the period in which the government of which I was the head was in office, we expended in this country on social security sums far and beyond those which had ever been expended before. My hon. friend who is sitting beside me did more on behalf of social security-and I am measuring this on the basis of the amounts which were made available in this connection-than had ever been done before under any other government in a period of 50 years or more. He will deal with that in detail, later. We increased the amount of social security benefits, old age pensions, soldiers' pensions, old age security payments and so on. In 1919, the Liberal party promised health insurance, and they won several elections afterwards on the strength

of their promise. They finally brought it in in 1957, subject to a qualification that it would require the consent of the majority of the provinces. That is as far as they went. When we came in it was one of the things which added to the difficulty of the financial situation in which we found ourselves, the amount of the expenditure we had to make in this connection in the first year being about $170 million and increasing year by year thereafter. If it had not been for the increases in social security payments and the assistance given to the provinces to enable them to discharge their responsibility, we would have had a deficit in no one year between 1957 and 1962.
A belief in social security and social justice is not something I have acquired in recent years. I have taken the same stand throughout. All of us are affected by the days of our childhood and youth, and I fully realize what the difference would have been had there been in effect something of the social security that was beginning to expand among all political parties after 1926.
As far as many social security matters are concerned, it is of interest that the government of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett brought in legislation on hours of work and vacations with pay as well as an unemployment insurance measure. But when the Liberal party came into power in 1955 the first thing they did was to submit the matter to the courts and to appoint counsel to argue that these measures were unconstitutional. Then they took years thereafter before introducing similar measures.

I believe now as I said in 1944, we must go forth to new horizons of social justice. Today the opportunity comes to us as it has come to few men in few generations to take part in the forward march of the common man. Tremendous changes are taking place. The state must guarantee and underwrite equal access to security, to education, to nutrition and to health to all. That assurance is inexorable through the awakening of the spiritual being of man everywhere, and the recognition by all men of their responsibilities for the welfare of every other man, not only within their own state but beyond its confines.
I am not going to give the quotations today because there will be fuller opportunity later; but throughout we in this party have followed the course of expanding social security in this nation. When we came into office the human betterment needs of Canadians had been neglected to such an extent that Canada lagged behind most of the nations in the western world in the care of those who, through no fault of 28902-5-1504
Canada Pension Plan
their own, were unable to meet even their most modest needs. Not once but twice in the five years we were in office we increased old age pensions, blind, disability, war veterans and other pensions. We brought these matters before parliament in order to rectify the dilatory tactics of the former administration in meeting a serious social security problem.
I am not going into the statistical record, but during our period in office we increased human betterment payments from the national treasury to the average Canadian by about 80 per cent. That is a record which indicates something of our purposes, our aims and our intentions. All of these things, disabled pensions, extra old age assistance and so on, will be dealt with by others in this debate. I shall do no more than refer to this fact. In the field of health and welfare the amount of payments in 1956-57 was $885 million and in 1962-63 expenditures were $1,900 million, an increases of 115 per cent. And so I could go on citing the whole field of social justice during a time when many argued that there should not be any expansion in social security however far behind other nations we had fallen up to 1957.
Mention was made of the United States by the hon. lady. It is perhaps useful to compare the position of Canada in relation to the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand. It is very difficult to get comparable data. The data for 1949-50 and 1956-57 are not exactly comparable with that for 1958-59 and 1959-60. But these are the figures. In 1949-50 the percentage of Canada's national income expended on social security was 7.8. In 1956-57 it was 8.7 per cent and by 1960-61 it was approximately 12 per cent. Some figures for other countries are: the United Kingdom, 12.5 per cent; New Zealand, 13.9 per cent and the United States 7.6 per cent.
I said a moment ago that no one had a monopoly of the feeling for others. I remember so well, however, the attitude and philosophy of the Liberal party in 1957 when the then member for Eglinton protested that the slight increase of $6 would not be effective until July 1. A moment ago the hon. lady said there should not be an increase in an election year. They did it themselves that year. They thought they could get away with $6, and the same group of six-buck boys is riding again. This time they promise a manna in the future. At that time I expressed myself in these words, as found on page 2774 of Hansard for March 28, 1957:
As far as old age pensions are concerned, we believe the increase is totally inadequate for the needy; it is niggardly and paltry. Twenty cents a day will do nothing to help the needy among the old age pensioners of this nation. The increase

Private Bills
of $6 per month simply will not meet their desperate need; and with the government spending so extravagantly and so profligately in other directions there are no words with which one could describe its disregard of the needs of our senior citizens.
We proceeded to increase these pensions subsequently. One of the most unusual explanations that was given by anyone opposite was made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). You know, he believes in two flags, and one thing and other like that. I am sorry he is not here today. On October 25, 1957, when we increased the old age pension by $9 a month, he said as found on page 427 of Hansard,-and listen to this for a philosophy:
I am going to support it, but it does present a real problem for all of us who are conscientious representatives of constituents on the Atlantic seaboard. The effect of the legislation the government is now proposing will be-perhaps not for anyone more than myself and the hon. members for Burin-Burgeo and Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador-to give to the retired adults in many of our communities larger incomes than those of the working members of their families who have to contribute through the sales tax toward the payment of these pensions.
There was a philosophy. Only one with a two-flag mentality could come out with an ejaculation like that.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay passage of this bill but I wish to mention a question of principle which was very much discussed in committee and which it might be useful to put on public record. May I first say that the members of the committee were greatly impressed with the presentation made by the sponsors of the bill, both in this house and in the other place, and with the very able assistance we received from the parliamentary counsel.
The question of principle to which I want to make reference is that incorporated in the proposed clause 8A (2). If I might summarize it in this way, there is conferred upon the central body the power itself to incorporate further corporations, thereby involving a delegation of the crown's right to incorporate. At the time the committee considered this there was general agreement among members, including the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and hon. members on this side of the house, that they were concerned about the possibility that a number of precedents might be set up, by which this power might be more greatly used.
At the time it was considered in committee it was disclosed to us that there had been three other examples in which this particular power had been conferred, all in connection with religious institutions, and it was agreed by all members of the committee

that the Ukrainian National Federation of Canada was no less entitled to this power. However I think I am expressing the views generally held by members of that committee in saying they would be unhappy to see this particular provision being brought forward in connection with other organizations whose beneficial purposes and bona fides are less obvious than they were in this particular case.
Therefore I would like to lodge a caution, for the benefit of others who might be bringing bills forward, that there is a general feeling that this particular power, that of delegating to a corporate body the right itself to create corporations, should not be too widely used in bills brought before this house.
Clause 1 agreed to.
Bill reported, and read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) that 75 per cent of the ownership of the stock of this proposed corporation will be held by Allstate Life Insurance Company, a United States company. Twenty five per
Private Bills
cent will be held by Simpsons-Sears Limited of Canada. The situation is that Allstate Life, the United States company, is actually owned 100 per cent by Sears-Roebuck, and the Canadian company of Simpsons-Sears Limited is 50 per cent owned by Sears-Roebuck; so it works out that about 87 4 per cent of the stock will be issued to the United States Allstate Life firm. That actually will not be the way it will be, but in effect that will be the equitable ownership. As to the remaining 12-2- per cent, Simpsons Limited of Canada will own it. There is another provision with respect to non-voting participating preference stock, 8 per cent of which will go to employees, who of course might be Canadians; so there may be Canadian ownership of somewhat more than 124 per cent, depending on the result.
Perhaps I should give a little more elucidation in view of the hon. member's question. Bill No. S-28, to incorporate this new Canadian life insurance company with the English name of Allstate Life Insurance Company of Canada and, in French, Allstate du Canada, Compagnie d'Assurance-Vie, is similar to Bill No. S-12 introduced at the last session, which bill was not passed prior to dissolution. The only change is in the addition of the French name. As many hon. members know, Allstate is the name of two insurance companies in the United States. They are, as I said, both owned by the Sears-Roebuck company. In January of 1953, when Sears-Roebuck and Simpsons Limited formed Simpsons-Sears Limited, there was an informal agreement or understanding that Simpsons-Sears Limited would eventually acquire an interest in the insurance business in Canada of the two United States Allstate companies. In pursuance of this agreement there was incorporated by parliament in 1960 the Allstate Insurance Company of Canada, which was given power to write all lines of insurance in Canada other than life. At the present time both United States companies-that is, Allstate Insurance Company, which writes all types of fire and casualty policies, and the Allstate Life Insurance Company, which writes life policies-are carrying on business in Canada very successfully. Their history in Canada is that in 1949 the fire and casualty company acquired a licence under the Foreign Insurance Companies Act and commenced its operations here on a major scale in 1953. Its annual premium volume is now in excess of $16 million, representing about 4.8 per cent of all automobile insurance in Canada, and a much lower percentage of fire and casualty lines. This company has approximately 250,000 Canadian policyholders at the present time; that is, the fire and casualty company. In 196o' the other company, the life company, acquired

Private Bills
a licence, also under the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, permitting it to write life policies in Canada.
The Allstate Life company has approximately $32,500,000 of life insurance in force in Canada at the present time, with approximately 3,400 policyholders. It is the business of this life company that it is proposed shall be acquired by the incorporation contemplated in this bill. If the incorporation of this Canadian life insurance company be granted, then it is intended that the holdings of the United States Allstate Life Company in Canada shall be transferred to the new Canadian company as of January 1, 1964.
I may say to the hon. member that the Allstate offices in Canada, both firms, are now staffed 100 per cent by Canadians. In addition several Canadians have gained their experience here and now fill important executive positions with the company in the United States. Allstate now employs about 700 people in Canada and it is expected that in the next five years they will employ about 1,000 Canadians. The company maintains offices in most cities of Canada and it is well known. It also maintains sales offices in the Simpsons-Sears department stores. In 1960 the Sears-Roebuck company and Simpsons-Sears Limited-I know this is rather confusing-carried on discussions as to the implementation of the informal agreement they made in 1953. After these discussions the Sears-Roebuck company offered to sell to Simpsons-Sears Limited an interest, not exceeding 50 per cent, in the Canadian business of Allstate; but Simpsons-Sears Limited, in view of its capital commitments, certain commitments it had undertaken for extending its mail order and departmental store business, decided to purchase a 25 per cent interest. To permit Simpsons-Sears to acquire this interest it was decided to incorporate Canadian companies which would acquire the Canadian Allstate business. The shares of these companies would be owned, as I said, as to 75 per cent by Allstate and, through Allstate, by Sears-Roebuck and Company, and as to 25 per cent by Simpsons-Sears Limited. As the shares of Simpsons-Sears are in turn owned 50 per cent by Simpsons Limited and 50 per cent by Sears-Roebuck and Company, this will result in Simpsons Limited having, as I say, 12| per cent interest, and Sears-Roebuck an 87i per cent interest in the Canadian business of Allstate. These percentages were arrived at without taking into account the 8 per cent interest represented by non-voting participating preference shares which will be held primarily by Canadian employees in the Simpsons-Sears profit-sharing fund. So it 
will readily be seen, Mr. Speaker, that both the Allstate companies have the right to do business in Canada, in any event, and that by the formation of the two Canadian companies and transfers of assets to them there will result somewhat more than 12J per cent Canadian ownership of the Allstate business, where there is presently no ownership whatsoever.
The two Canadian companies-that is, the one already incorporated and the one proposed by this bill-will each have nine directors, a majority of whom must under the law be' Canadian citizens residing in Canada. The original directors of this company, the ones applying for this incorporation, are all Canadian residents and five out of six of them are Canadians. It is planned that Mr. John Atkinson, a Canadian, shall be president of the two Canadian companies and that the management will continue to consist wholly of Canadians. The operation of the Canadian companies will to a large extent be carried on independently of the United States companies, which is consistent with the United States companies' intention to decentralize their operation. It will readily be seen by all hon. members, Mr. Speaker, that the acquisition of an interest in the Allstate business was an inducement to Simpsons Limited back in 1953 to enter into the agreement with the Sears-Roebuck company, and that this proposed incorporation will falcilitate the proper carrying out of this undertaking which the Allstate and the Sears-Roebuck people made at that time to the Canadian firm. Mr. Speaker, if the new life insurance company is not incorporated, the life business will have to continue as at present wholly-owned in the United States. Or in the alternative, it will have to seek a provincial incorporation, and that would be less desirable than a Canadian charter in the view of the applicants, the petitioners.
The present Canadian management and staff are most anxious to obtain separate Canadian incorporation. This will provide a much greater sense of identity than is possible at the present time when the Canadian operation is being carried on as a branch of the United States company. Incorporation in Canada will also permit a separate Canadian profit-sharing plan to be developed which, in view of the faster rate of growth of the Canadian part of the business over that in the United States, should prove highly advantageous to Canadian employees. They are the ones who want this incorporation and are most enthusiastic about Canadianizing it. That is another reason for the dual name.
I submit to all hon. members that there is some gain here in the form of at least a one

eighth Canadian participation in the ownership. It is not a large gain but it does give Simpsons Limited a fixed and definite interest in the life insurance operations in Canada of the Sears-Roebuck operation where none now exists. If the bill receives second reading it is my intention to move that it be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce, where it can be examined in detail.

He would like to Canadianize the Allstate company, but the owners and stockholders remain nevertheless foreigners and this, on the very day when we are informed that the American government has just imposed a 15 per cent tax on American investments in 22 countries of the world including Canada.
There are now in our country many life insurance, fire insurance and automobile insurance companies, several of which are Canadian undertakings, if we consider their staff as well as the capital invested.
Now, the staff of the company the incorporation of which is proposed may be Canadian, but on the other hand, the capital stock is 87-| per cent American-owned; in other words the profits it makes will go to foreign countries.
What is the amount of money that will flow out of Canada each year? I wonder whether the hon. member sponsoring this bill has given a thought to that before introducing the bill. What is the amount of benefits that will go out of Canada each year to be distributed to the owners of the stock of this company? Of course substantial amounts will be added to those that are already flowing out of this country. In fact, an estimated amount of over $1,200 million is leaving Canada every year to be distributed to citizens in foreign countries, in the form of profits, interests, benefits and dividends.
As the majority of owners of this company are citizens of the United States, they will be anxious to draw their benefits and to bring them back, so to say, to their own country.
Mr. Speaker, there are several Canadian companies selling insurance. Then why should we accept all foreign companies which would like to enter into the insurance business in Canada. In fact, it would be interesting to inquire of the Department of Finance or the department of insurance in Ottawa

On the other hand, I would be curious to know how many Canadian companies are doing insurance business in United States. In fact, is the American government willing to incorporate in United States a Canadian company wishing to do business there, especially in the insurance field.
It would also be interesting to know how many Canadian companies derive profits from the United States. As a matter of fact, I am convinced that the Canadian people would be amazed to note the disproportion in that connection. It would then be realized that Americans can set up companies in our country-which they use as their hunting grounds-in order to invest their capital, collect premiums and have them yield profits for themselves, while we are unable to avail ourselves of the same advantages.
If we asked ourselves all those questions, we might be less interested in incorporating so-called Canadian companies, which are only Canadian through their insurance salesmen. It must be kept in mind that it is the salesman who does all the work, while the shareholder does not even live in Canada. In fact, he receives dividends, he takes profits, but the insurance salesman is the one who does most of the work, and in a field where competition is rather fierce today. And those who benefit, who make large profits, are foreigners after all.
Let no one tell us that these are Canadian companies, when 87 per cent of the shares are held by non-resident Americans or others.
Mr. Speaker, I have nothing against the Americans. The United States have a population of 180 million people and, in my opinion, the Americans should be happy to sell insurance to their fellow citizens, leaving Canadians to do the same to their own people.
One must not forget that insurance companies represent one of the largest savings and investment funds for the development of a country's economy. Consequently, let us leave to our Canadian companies the task of keeping for us that savings and investment fund that will contribute to the growth of our economy.
Today, President Kennedy announced during the noon hour, that the United States government will be asked to approve a 15 per cent tax on American investments in

Canada. On the other hand, we will continue to export our capital to the United States and to invest there for the advantage of American companies. That is illogical, Mr. Speaker.
This afternoon, the Minister of Finance complained about his biggest headache, the deficit in our international balance of payments. It now seems that the members of his own party wish to add to his troubles by helping again those companies to take our capital away from us.
I now see the minister of commerce (Mr. Sharp), who is also interested in the development of trade and industry in this country. Insurance is one of the greatest businesses, one of the most important industries of the country. Then why encourage the establishment of foreign industries and businesses in our country when it would be perfectly possible to develop an insurance industry here in our country by Canadians and for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the sponsor of the bill will understand that such a situation is no longer justified. The sponsor of the bill will understand that we cannot in good faith accept the passage of a bill which would be giving still another part of our savings to foreign companies the profits of which will revert to non-residents and consequently leave the country.
Mr. Speaker, needless to say that an attempt can be made to have the bill read for the second time before the end of the session, but we shall not allow it to pass. Therefore, if the sponsor of the bill will realize that the time of the house is too valuable for that, he will simply withdraw his bill. It must be understood that if insurance companies were scarce in Canada, if there were not any, it would be different. But, we have enough especially in the field of life insurance; there are Canadian companies in the province of Quebec, as well as in all other provinces, with Canadian stock. Since we have enough and that we are in a position to develop that industry ourselves, to bring other foreign companies to Canada to operate in that field is utterly nonsensical and illogical.

It is not a question of stopping a Canadian citizen from taking out an insurance policy with the company of his choice. No, that is not the problem.
