speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had just about covered the preliminaries preparatory to discussing the particulars of the plan brought before the house. I might summarize. Mention had been made by the minister that the day of introducing old age pension increases before an election was over. I had just pointed out that in 1957 that was the course followed by the St. Laurent government, the increase becoming effective after the election with the results that everybody recalls at this time. I further pointed out that the reason given by the leaders of Liberalism in that year for the picayune amount that was provided for was, to use the words of the then minister of finance, "That is the way you fight inflation." This was his answer to criticism directed at the fact the pension would not be effective until July 1.
I should like to point out something more in that connection. During the period from 1953 to 1957 the provinces, and indirectly the municipalities, were being starved by the government of that day. The old age pensioners were being starved. The veterans were being starved. Then, after the election of 1957 we introduced appropriate additions and the members of the former government expressed different views, the general purport of which was, that one of the best ways of getting along is to recognize that you have to change your views. These remarks were made by one of the most distinguished members of the former government, and an equally distinguished member of the present government.
Now, sir, the attitude of the opposition was very clearly set forth during the period we were in office and also during the campaign. We stated we would extend social security; we would add to the dignity and security of our older citizens; we would make retirement from toil and labour a rewarding part of life through an addition to the present old age security program by bringing about directly an old age and retirement plan with survivor benefits. We said that we would cooperate with the provinces to bring about portable pensions. In addition to that, and

Canada Pension Plan
in order to assure survivor benefits, we would have to secure an amendment to the constitution. We endeavoured to secure that amendment for two years, in particular from January 17, 1962, thence during the next year until the time we were defeated in the house.
I might summarize the letters which were sent to the various provincial governments by me as prime minister. They were to the effect that the law officers of the crown advise that the authority, under the amendment to the British North America Act, section 94(a) in 1951, would permit parliament to enact directly graduated old age pension schemes, but would not permit the inclusion of benefit payable under certain circumstances to widows and children, nor to contributors who become disabled before they are old. To extend the law in this most desirable way, it would be necessary to replace the present section of the British North America Act in this way:
It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to
(a)	old age pensions, and
(b)	pensions and other benefits incidental to, or conducive to the better operation and administration of, a scheme of old age pensions,
We had hoped that agreement would have been reached by 1962 on a means of amending Canada's constitution, but we found it was impossible to secure agreement. The attitude of the provinces in general was favourable to our request, with the exception of one province and to a lesser extent a second, so that again under the constitution the dead hand of the past controlled the present to a degree that made impossible the bringing into effect of national social security legislation, providing for survivor benefits.
In this case the government has become a convert only in recent days to the need for consultation with the provinces, but in this legislation it is placing the cart before the horse. It has brought in a general plan in a resolution, and having brought in the plan, complex as it is, then it calls the provinces together to discuss the matter. I do not know what the reaction of the provinces will be, but certainly two of them have passed legislation in connection with pensions, legislation that may well become a dead letter unless there is full co-operation between the two levels of government, federal and provincial. These things have to be worked out so that in reality, as we debate the matter at this time, not knowing what tomorrow will bring forth in the meeting of the dominion and provincial representatives, we can only discuss in a general way the recommendations and suggestions made.

We intend to examine this matter most carefully. The minister has pointed out that it is complex and difficult. I understand one of its architects was Mr. Stanley, upon whom the Minister of Finance relied with such disastrous results in preparing the budget. After the fiasco of that budget and the recommendations made, it will be doubly necessary to give the fullest examination to this plan that he and those associated with him evolved, to the end that the government will be saved from itself once more and from having to make a further retreat.
After pleading for discussion freed from the sinister influence of political considerations, the minister asked for co-operation. We are going to give the fullest co-operation, and in a little while, Mr. Chairman, I will indicate how far we are prepared to go in this connection in order to give those who now sit on the government benches the opportunity of voicing their vote as they voiced their views in regard to social security during the election campaign.
Over the week end I read the biography of Arthur James Balfour, prime minister of the United Kingdom and a leader in Britain for almost 50 years. In the book there is an extract which illustrates the spirit we are going to use and apply as we examine this general plan. I quote:
Society is becoming more and more sensitive to the evils that exist in its midst;-
This would be around 1903-04.
-more and more impatient of their continued existence. In itself this is wholly good; but, in order that good may come of it, it behoves us to walk warily.
If only the Minister of Finance had read those words before he produced that budget.
It is, no doubt, better for us to apply appropriate remedies to our diseases than to put our whole trust in the healing powers of nature, but it is better to put our trust in the healing powers of nature than to poison ourselves straight off by swallowing the contents of the phial presented to us by any self-constituted physician. And such selfconstituted physicians are about and in large numbers-
It applies today, Mr. Chairman.
-gentlemen who think that they pay Providence a compliment by assuming that for every social ill there is a speedy and effectual specific lying to hand; who regard it as impious to believe that there may be chronic diseases of the body politic as well as of any other body ... Of two evils it is better, perhaps, that our ship shall go nowhere than that it should run upon the rocks.
All of us recognize the need for action being taken. As the minister has stated, there is universal agreement in that connection; but I have a number of questions to ask the government, and after all, Mr. Chairman, when you remove the halo from what has been said to date and start to look at the substance you

ask yourself: Is there not a great deal in what has been said which is of a nature expressing the possibility of a hope, while denying at the same time the achievement of that hope at an early date?
As the minister has said, this is a tremendous problem and I have a number of questions which I ask merely for information. I am sure the provincial premiers would find some of the answers very helpful.
With the taking over in large measure of the responsibility of providing all employed Canadians with a retirement pension, will private pension plans, in the natural sequence, not tend to be wiped out? It is a frightful challenge. There are hundreds of thousands of people who have pension plans, but not one word was said today, except by way of generality, as to what is going to be done with them.
Can any person under a private pension plan opt out of the national scheme?

speechtext:
That is an idea with considerable wisdom in it. We want to see the election campaign promises carried out. Before I deal with the thoughtful suggestion of the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler), may I refer to the Financial Post in this connection. I am not saying I am in agreement with these views, but they show how we must

carefully study this matter and not be stampeded into passing something that is going to be an incubus on the Canadian economy for years to come. We believe in the objective. We carried it so far that we increased social security payments during the period of our office by 79 per cent. But this is a very difficult matter, and we found after the examination not only by Dr. Clark but also by outstanding civil servants that there were many problems in the way. The Financial Post said:
There can be no doubt that the goal of portable pensions for all Canadians is a commendable one and well worth working for. Rarely now does a worker stay in one job for life. Indeed, a fastchanging economy demands a mobile work force and the loss of pension rights when moving from one job to another creates unnecessary hardship for the individual and unnecessary burdens for the nation as a whole-
Even getting a provincial portable pension plan working will impose many complications, most of them costly, on employers and employees. In Ontario, which has set up the first provincial program and scheduled its start for Jan. 1, 1965, companies are having difficulty fitting existing plans into the government's over-all pension framework.
Quebec now says it intends to introduce a plan similar to that scheduled for Ontario. British Columbia and Alberta are known to be actively considering comparable schemes.
Then it says this:
Inadequate study and over-anxious politicking could very well produce a pension mess beyond imagination and beyond repair.
I believe, as the minister said, that there is general agreement on the necessity; but the difficulty will be to work out a plan that is effective, constitutionally proper or co-operatively implemented with provincial assistance. The increase in the cost of living is now starting ahead faster than was the case when we were in office. They used to say what terrible things would happen when we borrowed money from the international monetary fund, but now they have done the same. The United States today is securing the right to borrow $500 million from the international monetary fund. This is the first time the United States has done that and it is bringing in regulations-if congress passes them, but effective now-designed to bring about that which we brought in in May of 1962. We had to take that action.
However, there is one group which needs assistance now, and that is the old age pensioners. Why not do that which was undertaken implicitly or indirectly by the former government in the elections of 1962 and 1963? There was a commitment. We on this side lost tens of thousands of votes because we stated: "We have raised you to $65. The other people raised you $6. We raised you from $46 to $65, and there will be an increase when the situation improves; but in the

meantime there will be this contributory system over and above the existing pension". The Liberal party said there would be an immediate payment. I say, very well, first of all, do not try and apply closure to the opposition. Do not try to lead the old people of this country to believe that the reason they are not going to get another $10 is because the opposition dared discuss the rest of this question. If it cannot be brought in immediately, make it effective now, and whenever the whole system is in effect then give each one the persion, beginning today. Then they would be doing something along the line they promised.
Second, we suggest that people be allowed to obtain their pension on an actuarially reduced basis as early as age 65. Is this plan actuarially sound? If it is actuarially sound and it is certified so, then we need not expect an ever-increasing levy on business, employers and employees, as has been the case elsewhere. By allowing our people before age 70 to obtain a pension at a reduced rate for the rest of their lives, no significant cost would be imposed on the federal treasury. Persons choosing to take their pension at an earlier age would, of course, benefit from any increase in pensions voted by parliament. While this was not said, it seems to me implicit in what the minister said that this $10 is the last increase. Because she mounted the white charger of political purity and said that never again are Canadians to be bought by their own money. The Liberal government of Mr. St. Laurent tried to do just that and put off the implementation of the additional pension till after the election so that the carrot would dangle before the voters of Canada. Also include a system of flat survivor benefits payable to widowed mothers and dependant children of widowed mothers. As I listened to the minister I think that something in this regard is being done. Canada is one of the very few countries in the western world which does not have a system of survivor benefits unrelated to a means test. Indeed, it is the view of Dr. Robert Clark that this is the greatest gap in the welfare legislation of Canada.
The basis of financial survivor benefits should be made the same as that used to finance old age security itself. This in turn should be altered from its present illogical basis as we see it to an equal tax on earnings of employers and employees, as is done in the United States under the social security act, and under this the self-employed would be covered under similar legislation.
With regard to co-operation with the provinces, the federal government should cooperate with the provincial governments in the regulation of pension plans. It could do
Canada Pension Plan
so in its capacity as an employer by seeking to have federal employees covered under provincial statutes. It could also offer to administer provincial portable pension acts for those provinces which were willing to pass the appropriate legislation, and a fee could be charged for this purpose.
The question of cost is one to which we must return-not the cost of the firm, fixed old age pension but this contributory one. Because experience has shown that governments have to plan most carefully if they are to assure that their pension plan will be as cheap as employee pension plans in the long run. In addition to that, as I said earlier, we would set up a contributory plan following the most careful study, to the end that the mistakes which have been found to exist in other such plans will be found wanting in ours.
I mentioned a moment ago that I should like to read this literature because it gives one an idea of events so very recent. I outlined a moment ago the promises made. Here is one which went across the country. The great trouble is that a lot of people read the big print but do not read the fine print. How often it happens that those who do not read the fine print find, after they have come to certain conclusions, that the results were not in keeping with the promises of the large print. This is one: "Jobs Created. Take a Stand for Tomorrow-Vote Liberal".

Here is what appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune: "What can we expect from the Liberals?" that paper asks. I see the Prime Minister smiling. He would go into office, the article says, with a tough schedule for the first 60 days of business, including a visit to London to meet Prime Minister Macmillan, a meeting with President Kennedy and arrangements for a budget by mid-June. Well, I tell the right hon. gentleman that the Hyannis Port honeymoon ended today as far as the United States is concerned. I want to give hon. members opposite an opportunity to support their ideals. We realize that an amendment to the effect that $75 should be paid would be one which would be out of order. But there is nothing to prevent a recommendation, and I know they are just waiting for an opportunity to be able to show that they want to recommend to the government immediate consideration of this proposition. They promised the old age pensioners in Canada $75 a month in the large print. Then, in the small print, there were some evasions and qualifications. Their advertising was carefully designed to delude, and it succeeded. It could not have been more effective. Everyone took it the government intended to follow this through. Now I read in the Toronto Star of June 29 an article by Mr. Joe Scanlon

in which he sums up everything in advance- and he is fairly close to authoritative sources:
They have a plan that will lead to an immediate increase in the present pension and at the same time take the first step to a contributory pension plan.

What that means is that we should pass this potpourri as it is-get it through; then work will start and the tremendous organization which would be required would be set up. I should like to bring to your attention that the amendment, which reads as follows:
-and this house asks that the government give consideration to making the payment of such additional pension to commence on this date-
-is out of order for the following reasons.
It is out of order first, because as has already been said on more than one occasion by some who have preceded me, it would require an additional expenditure and therefore would disturb the balance of ways and means. It is next out of order because, if such additional pension were to be paid and to commence on this date, it would clearly be in contravention of the normal rule in the house, with which surely hon. members on the opposite side are familiar, in that a private member cannot under any condition move an amendment which requires the expenditure of public funds. This is clearly set out in Beauschesne's fourth edition, page 214, citation 249 which reads:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian Commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer.
One could go on to read the subsections of the citation, and I refer Your Honour to the third subsection, which I think has immediate application here, and which reads as follows:
An amendment declaring that government action in any matter should be taken forthwith and giving a direct order which, if approved by the house, would compel the government to adopt measures involving an expenditure of public money, could not be moved by a private member.
It would seem, sir, that that is a complete answer to the amendment which has been moved on this occasion, and I do not need

to go into the matter at great length because this is a rule which has always been respected in the house and does not require any further elaboration. For those reasons it seems to me that the amendment is clearly out of order.

The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and especially the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier), mentioned the illegality of the amendment and suggested that it would involve an expenditure of public funds. I respectfully submit that such is not the case because the object of the amendment introduced by the Leader of the Opposition is simply to invite the government to consider the opportunity to adopt subsequently a measure that would allow it to pay an additional amount of $10 a month. In my opinion, the adoption of this amendment would not require at once the expenditure of public funds, because, subsequently, it will be up to the government to introduce legislation in accordance with the amendment for the house to pass.
The simple fact of adopting the amendment does not mean to legalize it.
I am told that a measure requiring the expenditure of public funds can only be introduced by a minister of the crown. In order that that measure be enacted, the proposed resolution must be followed by legislation introduced by a minister of the crown.
The adoption of the amendment introduced by the Leader of the Opposition is, therefore, not out of order because it does not require an immediate expenditure. In fact, it is a matter of adopting an immediate principle which could subsequently involve the expenditure of funds, providing some legislation were introduced by a minister of the crown for that purpose.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Justice and other speakers on the government side have suggested that this amendment is out of order on the ground that it increases expenditures and that this is not within the competence of a private member of the house. I would suggest that we look at the last sentence of the resolution, which says that the expenditures under this plan shall be paid out of or reimbursed from contributions by employees, employers and self-em-polyed persons. The minister herself indicated this afternoon that the $10 a month will be paid some time in advance of the actual collection of contributions. That means, therefore, that the money will be advanced and will be later reimbursed from the contributions. It may be that in the minister's mind there is a gap of only the period from January 1 to October 1; but there is nothing in this resolution that says that the one shall only be payable January 1 and the other on October 1. In other words, all it says here is that the $10 a month shall be either paid out of or reimbursed from contributions, and there is nothing in this resolution that sets a limit on how much this reimbursement shall be.
Moreover, the passage of this amendment would not be mandatory upon the government. This asks the government to give consideration to making the payment of such additional pension commence on this date. In other words, if this amendment were passed it would be a suggestion to the government that when they bring down the bill which will follow the passage of this resolution they should insert a clause in the bill, if they so choose, making the payment of the $10 a month effective upon the passage of the bill, or even retroactive to this date, of July 18. This is not mandatory; this is simply a suggestion to the government since the government itself has not placed any date in this resolution as to when the old age supplementary pension payment of $10 a month shall be paid out of or reimbursed from these contributions.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order I would refer hon. members to page 216 of the fourth edition of Beauchesne, paragraph 4 of citation 250:
The fundamental terms of a money resolution submitted to the house with the governor general's recommendation upon which a committee of the whole is set up cannot be amended. Amendments will only be in order if they fall within the terms of the resolution. The procedure in committee on those resolutions follows in principle the procedure of the committee of supply, and amendments are
Canada Pension Plan
out of order if they are proposed with a view to substituting an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation.
I would suggest that the fundamental basis of this pension plan is being changed from one of financial responsibility to one of financial irresponsibility by the amendment proposed. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has made it quite clear that this is a contributory scheme; that the $10 supplement being proposed will be refunded or made good out of contributions which can only start in the fall of 1964. If this $10 supplement is to be paid out of those contributions there must obviously be a starting date which is not so early or so far back as in effect to outrun the contemplated contributions.
It is the proposal of the government to institute the payment of the $10 supplement at a time which will match the contributions received. A scheme such as is proposed in this amendment would have the effect of unmatching the contributions and the payment and changing this contributory pension scheme from one of financial responsibility involving, in the long run, no subsidy or payment out of public funds, into one which is financially irresponsible and calls for the inevitable payment of money, in the long run, out of public funds. It therefore contravenes the citation I have mentioned, and I submit it is out of order.

Mr. Chairman, I hope to be able to conclude my remarks this time. But this gives me an opportunity to emphasize once again that my leader, in asking me to speak in his place, refused an opportunity to make political capital to the detriment of our old people, as did the government party and the Conservatives.
On the other hand, I think that the Minister of Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh)
28902-5-151
Canada Pension Plan
placed herself in an unfavourable position by forgetting that she was in the house today and not on the hustings.
As for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), he made it a point to refer to the forties.
As usual, we heard today the government party saying: we are introducing legislation that the former party did not want to submit. We heard the former government saying: What you are proposing now, we worked it out.
Mr. Chairman, since they want to quote historical facts and statistics, what about the Social Crediters who, in 1930, requested an increase of old age pensions and family allowances? And our opponents said then that it was a utopia and that our heads were in the clouds. But today the two old line parties want to take credit for those measures and suggest that they were achieved by them.
If we really want to do some good, I feel it is time, since all parties request that measure, that we forego politics and give our senior citizens the protection they need.
However, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has gone a little farther today. She told us: the opposition party has been working for two years to give you something, and it got nowhere. But, with my government, within three months I will submit a plan.
Mr. Chairman, I am now convinced that what is submitted to us at this time is the result of three months' work only. And I am truly afraid that what happened with regard to the budget will repeat itself with this measure.
It is not enough for the party in power to say to the Canadian electors: we are giving you a plan, three cheers for us. I believe that when our fellow citizens have studied the pension plan, they will not cheer so loudly.
The farmer will say: What about me? What will happen to me? Did I not contribute also to the growth of my country?
At the same time, the fishermen will say once again that he is the sucker, because he is not given anything under this plan.
And the small store owner will think: "And I, what is happening to me? There is no mention about me in this pension plan."
And what about the service station owners, and so on-
It might happen too that the rich stockholder in the stock exchange wonders why

Canada Pension Plan
he is not included in that pension plan? But in his case, I am less worried because representations will be made in due course and because this class of people will know perfectly how to adjust to the new plan introduced by the government.
To all the small people whom I mentioned, the Minister of Health and Welfare might just say: "Applaud, we have fulfilled an electoral promise."
In view of such pusillanimity, not to say cynicism, I wonder where we are going.
But once more, tonight, we of the Social Credit party, must congratulate the government because, despite all its blunders, at least, it is doing something, and is not content, like a certain other party which has been turned out of office, to waste two hours of the time of the house and keep us from attending to the nation's business.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, even if we think that the increase from $65 to $75 is still inadequate, and that the social security legislation is also inadequate, we must give the people a chance to try and make the best of what is offered by the government. Our elder citizens need government protection and, today, we are happy to see that a movement is taking shape throughout the country, because the hon. members who have visited their ridings lately have no doubt noticed that almost 75 per cent of our elder citizens now depend only on their old age pension to live on to the end of their days. So at this time, we must commend the government although we hoped they would go further in their projects.
When I suggest that the government should go further, I think that family allowances must soon be considered. And since reference is made to the federal-provincial conference, I think it is high time to think about the situation of our old people, who are in need, because it is painful to see 65-year old persons forced to sell their homes in order to qualify for old age assistance. I think the government should really bring legislation forward to deal with this matter as soon as possible.
I also wish to remind the government that it is high time something was done to help needy mothers, and also the blind and the disabled. It can count on our entire support for any measure of that kind.
Not only is the government increasing the old age pension, it also proposes introducing a portable pension plan. It is not easy of course to discuss, to criticize, to approve a

bill, or even to make suggestions about it when we know nothing of its provisions. However, it may not be useless to point out, once more, that Social Credit has always stood for progress in that direction.
Since the minister has invited suggestions, when the time comes to debate the resolution, the government might even consider allowing people of 60 or more to benefit from this welfare measure.
I understand that, in certain industries that have a contributory pension plan, employees are entitled to their pensions as soon as they reach age 60. They can thus retire earlier, thereby making jobs available for young workers who are now unemployed. I know that many of our senior citizens would gladly retire at 60 if they could count on an adequate pension plan to provide for their needs from then on.
Mr. Chairman, there were several pension plans in private industry before this, but I believe that a uniform scheme throughout Canada would be of much greater interest. And why would it be so? Because first of all, it would enable a lowering of such insurance cost to a considerable degree and also give the individual the possibility of recovering his freedom, because we know that pension plans are a stumbling block for many people. I know, for instance, that many civil servants will say: "I might have a good job in private enterprise, but I cannot accept it, because, in five or ten years from now, I shall have my pension."
The same thing is said in private industry. In such a case, the worker is bound and cannot leave his job for a better paid one because he knows that he must remain where he is if he wants to benefit from his pension plan. We shall most certainly have suggestions to make about the provisions of this legislation when we are in possession of the bill.
We shall also have recommendations to make about the financing of the measure. The Social Credit party would undoubtedly have been able to suggest alternative means of financing which would have cost a lot less to the Canadian taxpayer. Finally, I hope to have an opportunity at that future time to answer the stock question of the Leader of the Opposition who just a few days ago again asked our leader "Where will you find that money?"
I hope, Mr. Chairman, to be in a position to take 20 minutes before long to explain in the clearest, simplest and most precise

terms where a Social Credit government would find the money to finance social legislation.
If we consider what we are offered today- the budget incident proved it-the only benefits that are offered our people today are given to them only after an extra third is to be paid by them in administration costs. The administration cost of the budget is today exactly the third of the budget amount. So, I believe that the occasion will be given to me to answer the Leader of the Opposition-and I shall not then prevent the other hon. members from listening to me carefully-because be it today, in five years or in ten years, I am sure that the house will ponder over that, as the capitalistic system we have today will, sooner or later, have to resort to a measure advocated by the Social Credit party if it wants to maintain individual enterprise and individual liberty.
What is surprising, Mr. Chairman, is that the two governments which succeeded one another in this house have in turn advocated measures which the Social Credit party has had for years while neither one nor the other dared-I say "dared"-launch the smallest experiment with the financial suggestions offered by my party.
Another feature of the contributory pension plan on which I must expand here is the one concerning its constitutional or unconstitutional character. I already see my hon. friends getting impatient and saying to themselves: Those Quebec demands again. It will come, Mr. Chairman, but not for the moment, because first of all, I wish to consider the matter as a federal member only, that is as a legislator of the country from sea to sea and then, I will be pleased to express the views of my province.
Some will say that any discussion at this stage is difficult because the Prime Minister has convened a federal-provincial conference on the matter. I do not quite agree, because I think this is the time to express our views to the Prime Minister if we want him to channel the discussion in that direction during the federal-provincial conference.
From the point of view of all provinces, the question that seems to arise is this: Why lose the opportunity of having at our disposal millions of dollars we urgently need for our own purposes? And that is, Mr. Chairman, the objection raised by Quebec. It could also come from Ontario, New Brunswick or any other province, because I am of the opinion that our provinces really need additional funds for their own undertakings today. One 28902-5-1514
Canada Pension Plan
province might be able to do without them, because I notice that in Alberta they have found a government that did not wait for the contributory plan to balance its budget.
Well, Mr. Chairman, to mention but one of the Quebec demands, here is according to Le Devoir, what Mr. Gerin-Lajoie said:
A universal pension fund would facilitate the establishment of a school credit board.
A pension plan under provincial control would put into the hands of the provincial government a sum of at least $250 million per year. Such an amount would facilitate investment operations not only for the provincial government but also for the institutions that rely on financial help from the province for their investments, such as school boards, municipalities, classical colleges and universities.
That is an example from Quebec. It could have come from Ontario or somewhere else.
Mr. Chairman, that is only an example to show how useful it could be for the provinces to have the control of the funds that would accumulate under the present act in the years to come.
The government will be able to listen favourably to that statement of principle, which has nothing to do with the constitutionality of the project, although it is not yet sure the provinces will approve it. But it seems that if the provinces manage their contributory pension funds themselves, they could come to a difficult but possible agreement, since portable pensions may result in difficulties, because of salary differences and various operations in the provinces.
That is the reason why I do not think the province of Quebec should take a different stand from that of the other provinces. It has only to put forward its claims and it is possible that they will be listened to carefully.
But, Mr. Chairman, I think that at the present time, the Quebec problem has not only to do with the claiming of this source of income. The program raises mostly a constitutional problem. The question is very serious for the province at this time.
Has the federal government the authority to legislate in that field? Many will be tempted to say yes since, after all, Ottawa already has legislation concerning old age pensions and unemployment insurance and since the proposed scheme is nothing but an extension of that social and labour legislation.
However, outraged citizens of Quebec will say in reply to that statement made in good faith: "If, one day, I had the stupidity to give you my tie, it does not mean that you now have the right to take my shirt away from me".

Canada Pension Plan
That is somewhat the position of the province of Quebec and that is the point which should be discussed. The provincial government sorely regrets having given away its legislative and taxation powers in the past. In a fit of nostalgia, it promptly rebels against any further encroachment by the federal government.
But that makes the other provinces impatient; they can hardly understand how one province can oppose legislation which seems acceptable to all of them.
I would like to make it clear to all hon. members that the province of Quebec is not really responsible for this situation. Once, it was given certain rights like all other provinces, and the province of Quebec wants to keep these responsibilities which are clearly established in the British North America Act.
Municipalities come under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Consequently, the Municipal Loans and Development Act is ultra vires. The province of Quebec is against it and who, in this house, can blame it.
I think that the civil rights come under provincial jurisdiction. But, by its portable pension plan, the federal government wants to pass legislation in that connection and Quebec is against that. Which member here could blame our province? No one, Mr. Chairman. If there are any, they will say it is inconceivable that one province should stand in the way of a stronger confederation.
I agree that Canada should be strong and that to be strong it must remain united.
It seems unfair that the province of Quebec should prevent nine other provinces from enjoying the development taking place throughout Canada, as it also seems unfair that nine provinces could object to the just claims of a province that is an equal partner within this same confederation.
There is a solution, Mr. Chairman. It is imperative while there is still time, that Canada, the provinces, the hon. members of the house, recognize merely the fact that the province of Quebec is simply not a province like the others. The province of Quebec is not asking more than the others, but it only wishes to preserve the rights that were granted to it by the British North America Act. This is not a privilege, Mr. Chairman, it is a right.
During the last election campaign, there was great hope in the province of Quebec. Mention was made of equality, of bicultural-ism, of bilingualism, of all kinds of words starting with bi- and a few weeks after the

opening of this parliament, we heard the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamon-tagne) state in high-sounding terms: "We shall be the fathers of a new confederation". Strange father of a strange confederation who, within two months, begot three children who are totally unacceptable to the province of Quebec.
Besides, it is a strange confederation, especially when the Prime Minister should have to decide, with his back to the wall, that the legislation will be considered at a federal-provincial conference. Those measures, so to speak, are the three children unacceptable to the province of Quebec. You know which ones I mean, but I shall name them: the plan to assist municipalities, the portable pensions scheme and the program of assistance to universities.
After that, people are surprised to see that the province of Quebec is so hard to please. During election campaigns, it is shamelessly misled; not only its rights are recognized, but some others are acknowledged that it does not even possess, for instance, the right to establish full bilingualism throughout the country. That is an achievement which every French Canadian, in his heart of hearts desires, but which is not based on any constitutional text. Instead of promising things to which Quebec has no right, let it rather get its due.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne), the new father of a new confederation, spoke in Quebec of giving French Canadians additional rights. And, as soon as he takes over, he rushes into a field which is dear to French Canadians. True to his former attitude, he advocates centralization and just keeps silent or goes out when things get too hot.
The solution, Mr. Chairman, as I said and repeat today, is simply to recognize that Quebec is not a province like all others.
Quebec never refused to pay taxes to the federal government, even when they were as hateful as the one on building materials. The province of Quebec was never opposed to any federal legislation, whatever it might have been, whether in the educational or any other field. Yet, it always said: "Give us an equal amount when you invade a field under provincial jurisdiction."
It is as simple as that, Mr. Chairman, a little comprehension, a little understanding on the part of the other provinces, and everything will be all right.
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, I wonder why it is always the opposition which should stand up for Quebec's rights.

To my mind it would be easy for the 40 or 50 members from the province of Quebec, who are sitting on government benches, to make suggestions to the government, when such questions are raised.
Allow me now to quote an article of Jean Marc Leger which appeared in he Devoir and which reads as follows:
And Our Members of Parliament
In the various Quebec-Ottawa disputes which stem in fact from a single conflict, what is going to be the position of our French Canadian members in the house? Their task will surely not be easy, but the moment of truth is nearing when they will have to choose between party and country. It is not sufficient to try lobbying, to have compromise solutions accepted, more often a graceful form of surrender. They will be judged by their stand, their speeches, their vote on important issues.
Mr. Chairman, I conclude these few comments by assuring the house that they have been made in the best possible spirit.
I truly hope that, during the federal-provincial conference, it will be possible to find a satisfactory means of respecting Quebec's demands without jeopardizing a piece of legislation which the other provinces wish with all their hearts.
Let us find a scheme under which one or two provinces could join the plan by means of an agreement while the others would have a similar program of their own and then all Canadians would benefit from legislation which, without being perfect, would none the less improve social conditions.
Then the Minister of National Health and Welfare will be able to say that she has given Canada an old age pension plan and our fellow citizens will be able to rejoice because, as I said, it will be a great improvement over the last five years. And this will be in the best interests of French Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that the Secretary of State will not only take up with his colleagues the question of bringing the legislation back to the house after the premiers have met, but that there will be at least one further day provided so that the chairman can rule on the amendment proposed tonight. To leave that amendment over for two weeks, let alone the possibility of leaving it over until fall, I submit is not only unfair to the house but is unfair to the people of the country.
I realize that the main subject before us is the introduction of a new scheme for provision of old age security and that we should not get

Canada Pension Plan
lost in the immediate matter of the $10 increase. But I think it is quite an accurate reflection of how the people of the country feel that the house has been in a bit of a turmoil tonight over this very question. My mail indicates that our older people across the country are assuming from the announcement about this legislation that their $65 cheques will go up to $75 almost any month now; yet we have been told today by the Minister of National Health and Welfare that the best that can be hoped for is that the $10 increase will take place some time early in 1964. I submit that that is not good enough in the light of all the promises made by the party now in power during the recent election campaign. While I admit that the performance tonight was a little lacking in decorum, and was perhaps not parliament at its best in terms of procedure, I suggest that it was a reflection of the strong feeling in the country that something should be done about this matter. It is not a case of how the chairman rules on the amendment or how the committee or the house might vote on the issue. We as private members put it to the government that they have to find a way to divide the question into its two parts and get this $10 increase through to our old age pensioners at the earliest possible date.
I said at the outset that this proposed legislation marks, in my view, the entry of this country into a new and extremely important phase of the whole question of old age security. I have down in my notes three one-word headings describing the history of old age pensions in Canada as I see it. I take a certain amount of personal interest in the fact that I think the effective history of old age security in Canada actually began on the day I was born. It just so happens that on June 18, 1908-most hon. members will remember a more recent June 18-the House of Commons gave second reading to and debated in committee the Government Annuities Act, which was the first piece of legislation providing anything in the way of old age security for the people of this country. That is an interesting debate to read. The proposal was for an annuity of a maximum of $50 a month. There were the usual arguments about the danger of this interfering with private business and the danger of its doing something about the initiative of the people, and so on. Concern was expressed about the cost. The minister piloting the bill tried to allay the fears of hon. members of that day by saying that it would cost the government only $50,000 a year. However, it got started. But what got started then was the recognition of the fact that something needed to be done by government to assist

people in their old age. That phase-I call it recognition of the need-took a long while. It started in 1908, though there had been agitation even before that.
Some years later, in 1926, the Old Age Pensions Act was passed, which provided a pension of $20 a month payable at age 70 on a means test. Then as hon. members know, through a number of years efforts were made to get the pension increased, and finally it got up to $40 a month. But that phase, which lasted roughly from 1908 down to about 1950, was merely a phase in which we recognized that government had to do something about the needs of our older citizens.
Then in 1950 we moved into the second phase. That second phase I characterize with the word "universality". If there is one thing to be said about the report of the old age security committee of 1950 and the legislation which came out of the recommendations of that committee, it is the acceptance of the principle that in old age there should be something for everybody in the country, without any means test. As I say, it took us many years to reach that point; but we did reach it in 1950 or 1951, when the legislation was passed, becoming effective in 1952, and we established the fact that pensions for senior citizens should be on a universal basis, that everybody should have a pension when he reaches a certain age. That was a tremendous step forward from the earliest phase, which was merely recognition of the need.
We have now come to the point where we realize that a further phase must be moved into, and that is the phase where we provide adequacy. The reason I welcome the legislation now before us is because I think it is a step-a halting step but nevertheless a step -in the right direction toward putting old age pensions on a basis of adequacy, of providing sufficient for a decent retirement.

My hon. friends across the way should not applaud too loudly, because all I am saying is that it is a good step. It does not provide adequacy; it only starts that direction and there is still a long way to go. If we are going to have a pensions scheme in Canada that provides adequate pensions for old age, there are a few things we have to face up to. First of all, I think we have to recognize the basic principle, the philosophy if you will, that older people who have finished their time of work are entitled not just to be kept alive by $20 a month, or $65 a month, or $75 a month, but to a standard of living equal to that which society is able to provide at the time of their retirement by those who are still working. I do not know

why we settled so long tor the silly notion that it was good enough for old people just to keep them alive. People who have done their share of producing the nation's wealth or developing the nation's economy are entitled in their retirement years to a standard of living equal to that which they themselves have helped to build up. Let us not go for this argument which sometimes appears in the editorials of some of our newspapers which is directed against the extravagance of old age pensions and the political auctioneering which is going on, and all the rest of it. What these arguments fail to recognize is that it is a sound philosophical principle, a sound principle of human life that we are trying to accept, when we say that we must move into an era so far as old age pensions are concerned when we can provide an adequate living standard.
The next thing we must recognize if we are going to do anything toward providing an adequate coverage is that it cannot be done by reliance upon private pension plans. I could expand on this but perhaps I can do no better than to quote a few sentences from Dr. Robert Clark, who wrote a monumental work a few years ago on old age security in the United States and Canada.
In paragraph 1504 of his report he says this:
The mere fact that so many hundreds of thousands of employees are now members of pension plans does not ensure that any given proportion of those who reach pensionable age will ever receive a pension.
In another paper the same Dr. Clark had this to say:
From the general viewpoint of the public interest that as many as possible of the aged should have an adequate income, and not merely a subsistence income, employee pension plans have two disadvantages, apart from the limitations of coverage referred to earlier. Under the majority of pension plans in Canada, when an employee leaves his employer prior to retirement he does not get any benefit from his employer's pension plan unless he has been with the employer for 10 years or more. Employees who change jobs many times in the course of their lives may work for a succession of employers with good pension plans, yet reach retirement with only a meagre pension to supplement their Old Age Security. Likewise undesirable from the above-mentioned viewpoint is the fact that the vast majority of employees covered by pension plans, confronted when they leave their employer with the choice of cash or a deferred annuity, take cash. As a consequence of these factors, to an extent which it is impossible to determine, most employee pension plans restrict the mobility of labour. Although the point Is readily exaggerated, most pension plans also give employers an incentive to discriminate in hiring personnel against persons over age 40. These disadvantages are likely to be more serious in noncontributory pension plans.
Yet despite the fact that authorities such as Dr. Clark have expressed such views as this-and Dr. Clark is not alone; we have a 28902-5-152
Canada Pension Plan
good many professors in this field in Canada who are speaking and writing most effectively on this subject-the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the paper she presented this afternoon says:
The Canada pension plan is not intended to be comprehensive in any other sense-
The reference back is to the intention that it should cover everybody.
It is not designed to provide all the retirement income which many Canadians wish to have. This is a matter of individual choice and, in the government's view, should properly be left to personal savings and to private pension plans-
Our whole point is that Dr. Clark is right. When you leave pension plans to private auspices they will not provide adequate coverage. We shall not move into the phase of adequacy if we leave this to private plans. We must enlarge tremendously the role of the public sector in the whole business. The Minister of National Health and Welfare was completely frank about it in her paper. In another place, where she talks about funding versus pay as you go, she says:
The absence of large reserves means that there will not be large transfers of funds from the private sector to the public sector.
Our contention is that we shall not move into this phase of development unless we accept a much greater measure of government responsibility than is envisaged in this plan. In this connection, I suggest that the people of Canada, about the third day after they have read of today's statement by the minister, will wake up to its inadequacies. Figures have been thrown at us today about possible pensions-a man and his wife would get $175 a month, both, perhaps, if both were contributing. This is made up of $100 under the Canada pension plan and $75 under old age security provisions. But this would be possible only in the case of persons whose income was $4,000 or more.

speechtext:
I thank the committee for its courtesy. Let me point out what will happen under the terms of this plan as it develops. The minister has made it clear that registration will not begin until May, 1964. Payments into the plan will not begin until October, 1964. Then, the white paper makes it clear that the first year in which any benefits can be drawn from the plan will be 1966, and in 1966 a person whose income has been

Canada Pension Plan
$4,000 and who has been contributing can get a pension under the plan amounting to $10 a month if he retires in that year at the age of 70. If he retires in 1967 he can get $20 a month. It adds up to this: not until 1975 will it be possible under this plan for a person to get a pension of $100 plus the $75 under the Old Age Security Act.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, after her little partisan and political introduction was over, said: let us not play politics with this whole question. Yet she has laid before us a plan which even under its present terms will not be fully effective for 12 years. During that time we shall have three, or possibly four federal elections- more, if we continue at the recent rate. Does the hon. lady suggest that we can get through all that period of time without having political arguments about this measure? I think it is nonsense to deprecate political discussion of this issue. What I think is wrong, though, is the kind of thing which happened today- the government giving the impression that it is going to pay $10 immediately, whereas it will not be paid until next year, and $175 in the near future when in actual fact that amount of money will not be available as a pension until 1975, and even then only to those whose income had been $4,000 a year.
All this underlines my point. I welcome the fact that we have made an initial, halting step in phase three. We have begun to develop a scheme whereby we could provide adequate pensions. The real goal, however, is years away and will remain many years away unless the government can get over this notion that, somehow, the greater part of our providing for old age must be left to private plans, insurance companies and so on.
I could hardly contain myself this afternoon, or tonight, when the Leader of the Opposition claimed that this plan would draw off all kinds of funds and take away the function of providing pensions from private plans, insurance companies and the like. That is precisely what it does not do. It provides a scheme under which people who are employees will pay 1 per cent of their wages into the plan. People are not used to pension plans costing so little and they know that for so little they will not get much in return.
In discussing the pay as you go plan versus a funding arrangement, the minister says the reason for the line which the government has followed is that it is not proposed that large reserves would be built up as a vehicle for federal debt management or investment. One could argue the respective merits of these two methods, and there are merits on both sides. There are strong arguments in

favour of a pay as you go scheme, but I suggest this should be viewed in the light of our whole economic problem, and one of the main elements of our problem today is securing public control of the economy of the country so that the savings of the people can be used for the advantage of the whole country. The way the government's plan is worked out, with all its sophistry about leaving large areas to private plans and individual choice, means that large amounts of the people's savings will still be in private hands, in the hands of the insurance companies to be used for investment in ways in which they think fit rather than the people deciding through their government on how they should best be used. I suggest these two things must be dovetailed together; the whole question of providing adequate pensions and of the funds which are saved being used in ways which are good for society as a whole through public investment.
I say, readily, that I think this is a most significant date in our history-a milestone. We have come 55 years in this story. We are now moving into phase three, but I do not think that after all these years we need to take such a halting step. The minister says that other countries have this sort of thing. Of course they have; even Sweden which has done very well, took a few years to get where it is today.

There is one thing that the minister said this afternoon with which I want to express wholehearted agreement and that is her drawing attention to the fact that there are other areas of need. She mentioned in particular widows with dependant children, disabled persons not yet 65 years of age and orphans. She was perfectly right in

pointing out that as circumstances now stand they cannot be dealt with under a federal plan for old age pensions, but I am glad that a conference is to be held with the premiers to discuss this sort of thing and I hope we will move with serious concern toward integrating our various welfare and pension plans to provide a decent life for our people.
I mentioned Dr. Robert Clark. There is Professor Clarence Barber of the University of Manitoba, there is Professor John Morgan of Toronto, there is Dr. Malcolm Taylor of the University of Alberta and there are others across the country who are experts in this field, not to mention the experts we have in our own public service, not to mention the tremendous interest in all of this by the people who work under the direction of the Canadian welfare council. I think we should get over this notion of just working on one piece of legislation today and another after the next election and thinking we have solved the problem. We have got to get together and integrate the whole program.
I welcome strongly the introduction of this legislation. I do not think I am overstating it when I characterize it, as I have tried to, as entering upon a new phase in old age security; but I hope we will soon step up our pace in this sort of thing, that we will really start to achieve adequacy in the old age field, that we will integrate it with the other aspects of social security and social welfare so that it will soon be really true that there is a good life for all our people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CANADA PENSION PLAN, INCREASED OLD AGE SECURITY PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate on the Canada pension plan. I am happy to hear that the spokesman for the New Democratic party and the spokesman for the Social Credit party are in favour of the plan. I regret, however, that again it is the Conservatives who are against this major piece of social legislation. History again is repeating itself.
This plan of social insurance, promised in our election campaign and delivered within the first 60 days of decision by the twenty sixth parliament of Canada by the courageous and enlightened leadership of the present Prime Minister, will increase the benefits to our senior citizens now and much more in the future as average wages and accumulated benefits increase. Members of this house will want, I am sure, to commend and thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare who has in so short a space of time worked and persevered with her advisers in the Department of National Health and Welfare to make this pension scheme possible. In the tradition of previous Liberal ministers of

Canada Pension Plan
national health and welfare the present minister is making available to the senior citizens of this country the benefits of the philosophy and the reform policies of the Liberal party, which strives for the attainment of security and dignity for every Canadian citizen.
In our industrial society the age of 65 is often being accepted as the compulsory age for retirement. Yet we are a work-oriented society. Unfortunately a man in retirement often loses not only his self-esteem and social responsibility but above all his financial income. The solution to this problem is not to throw to our senior citizens a bribe of a few dollars in old age pension before each election. The solution in the economic aspect of retirement is an actuarially sound contributory pension system with benefits designed to provide a decent retirement living. The Canada pension scheme is thus designed to give our senior citizens in retirement a comfortable living.
As the minister stated this afternoon, a realistic minimum level of pensions is too difficult to achieve in a country like Canada merely by increasing the flat rate pension. Living costs vary between city and village and between different regions of the country. The purpose, therefore, of the Canada pension plan is to make available reasonable minimum levels of income for all Canadians at normal retirement ages, and within the plan there will be room for the possible continuation and extension of other private pension plans to provide benefits over these minimum levels.
The main feature of the plan, Mr. Chairman, will provide a flat increase in the present old age pension from $65 to $75 per month at the age of 70. The $10 raise will be paid out of the fund and it is estimated to be $116 million per year. The earnings related portion of the pension based on contributions, plus the flat rate pension, would both be available at any age between 65 and 70 depending upon the choice of the contributing pensioner. The rate of contribution during the ten year transition period will not exceed 2 per cent of the earnings on which contributions are made, as stated previously by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, contributions will be deductible from income tax as now exists for private pension plans. Self-employed people will be encouraged to join the plan. They will pay the full 2 per cent of the first $4,000 of their earned income. At existing wage levels the total monthly pension available to a single person at age 70, whose average monthly pensionable earnings were $333 per month, will be $175 per month,

Business of the House which is comprised of a graduated contributory part of $100 plus the $75 per month flat rate pension.
An enviable feature of this Liberal plan is that at every level the Canadian pension will be higher than United States security payments. In comparison a United States citizen receives only $112 per month at the age of 70 based on monthly earned income of $333. I assure hon. members that the present plan will be entirely self-financing and therefore no burden at all will be placed on the national treasury. May I call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might ask the Secretary of State formally, now that Your Honour is in the Chair, if he will consider providing at an early date another day's debate on the resolution we have been discussing, so that the chairman of the committee of the whole could have an opportunity to give his ruling on the proposed amendment?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should be glad to bring that suggestion to the attention of my colleagues. I am sure hon. gentlemen realize that I could not vary the business the government had agreed upon in this way without consultation. I do not believe that I could recommend that we interrupt the consideration of budget resolutions, except possibly for the tax bills, until they are completed. Of course, the sooner they are completed the happier the government will be.
